description: We're a Bhopal-based team building a fire early-warning web app for the MODIS/VIIRS Hot Spots challenge. We turn NASA satellite fire data into a burning-activity calendar that helps responders act faster. Our lead works in ML, Python and React. Looking for data, frontend and design teammates. Let's build something that matters.
summary:
Kiln Watch is a satellite-data analysis platform that addresses a major challenge in long-term hotspot monitoring: MODIS and VIIRS sensors can report different hotspot counts because they have different spatial resolutions, detection characteristics, and observation opportunities. Comparing their raw observations directly can therefore create misleading trends.

Our team developed a harmonization workflow that uses NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS observations to build a more consistent historical reference record. The platform applies sensor-aware filtering, calibration across overlapping satellite records, statistical adjustment, and uncertainty estimates. Users can explore regional hotspot patterns, inspect detections, compare historical activity, and ask an AI-assisted analyst questions about the results.

Kiln Watch aims to make long-term hotspot analysis more transparent and useful for researchers, environmental analysts, and decision-makers. It does not replace NASA FIRMS or provide official fire warnings; it adds an evidence-based analytical layer to help users interpret changing satellite records.
details:
Kiln Watch is an interactive satellite-data analysis platform developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the challenge of harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS hotspot observations.

The problem: MODIS and VIIRS use different sensors, spatial resolutions, and detection characteristics. MODIS observations have approximately 1 km resolution, while VIIRS observations have approximately 375 m resolution. Their raw hotspot counts are therefore not directly interchangeable. A change in satellite sensor can appear as a change in fire activity, even when the underlying activity has not changed.

Our solution: Kiln Watch builds a harmonized historical record from NASA FIRMS observations. Its processing workflow uses sensor-aware quality filtering, observation-opportunity analysis, overlapping satellite records, calibration, statistical adjustment, and uncertainty estimation. It connects observations through a common reference scale and provides evidence that users can inspect rather than presenting adjusted numbers without context.

What users can do:

  • Explore historical hotspot activity across selected geographic regions.
  • Compare activity across years, months, and satellite records.
  • Inspect individual grid cells and their detection evidence.
  • Examine regional activity patterns and seasonal behaviour.
  • View historical activity comparisons through the platform's analysis tools.
  • Ask a Gemini-powered analyst questions about the results.
  • Export selected analysis and generate reports.

Validation and scientific approach: We tested the harmonization approach using a MODIS-denial experiment: calibrating on an earlier overlap period, withholding MODIS observations, and evaluating how well the method reconstructs a later period using VIIRS. Regional validation includes comparisons of raw and harmonized ratios, reconstruction error, rank correlation, and uncertainty intervals. The results also expose cases where the method under-corrects or performs less reliably, rather than hiding them.

Technology used:

  • Python and DuckDB for data processing and analytical queries.
  • FastAPI for backend services.
  • React and Vite for the frontend.
  • MapLibre GL JS and Three.js for geospatial and 3D visualisation.
  • Google Gemini for natural-language analysis.
  • GeoParquet and JSON/CSV for data handling.
  • MCP tools and n8n for tool integration and workflow automation.

Intended impact: Kiln Watch aims to help researchers, environmental analysts, and decision-makers interpret long-term hotspot patterns without confusing changes in sensor technology with changes in real-world activity. It is an independent analytical platform built using NASA data, not an official NASA product or fire-warning service.

Important limitation: Satellite hotspots represent detected thermal anomalies, not automatically confirmed fires or burned area. Kiln Watch provides historical analysis and uncertainty information; it does not claim to predict fires or issue official warnings.
